Controlling action counts per planning unit

Source: vignettes/Action_cardinality.Rmd
Action_cardinality.Rmd

add_constraint_action_cardinality() constrains how many individual actions are selected in each planning unit. It accepts the same sense, actions, and optional name conventions used by other constraint functions, together with count and the spatial scope pu.

sense Constraint in each scoped unit Example
"min" At least count actions At least one threat-management action
"max" At most count actions Capacity for at most four interventions
"equal" Exactly count actions Exactly two interventions

The function adds rules to a new problem object and preserves its input. Counts are integers, so exact counts do not use a numerical tolerance.

Define the actions 

problem <- create_problem(
  pu = data.frame(id = c(10L, 20L, 30L), cost = 7),
  features = data.frame(id = 1L, name = "woodland"),
  dist_features = data.frame(pu = c(10L, 20L, 30L), feature = 1L, amount = 100)
) |>
  add_actions(
    data.frame(id = c("restore", "control", "fence", "monitor")), cost = 1
  )

Without a cardinality rule, the optimizer keeps its default maximum of one action per unit. Registering action sets does not change that limit and does not create extra decisions: a set with two members contains two counted actions, even if one member also belongs to another set.

Different capacities in different units 

capacities <- problem |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(4, "max", pu = 10L, name = "capacity_10") |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(2, "max", pu = 20L, name = "capacity_20")
capacities$data$constraints$action_cardinality
#>                 type count sense        name actions pu
#> 1 action_cardinality     4   max capacity_10    NULL 10
#> 2 action_cardinality     2   max capacity_20    NULL 20

Unit 10 permits up to four actions, unit 20 up to two, and unit 30 keeps the default maximum of one. pu = c(10L, 20L) would apply a bound separately to both units, rather than limiting their combined number of actions. pu = NULL applies the rule to all currently registered units.

Require actions from a subset 

required <- capacities |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(
    1, "min", actions = c("restore", "control"), pu = c(10L, 20L),
    name = "habitat_or_threat"
  )

Each of units 10 and 20 must select at least one of restore or control. This count includes individual actions, rather than the number of registered sets. Supply action ids or the existing actions$action_set classification labels; identifiers registered by add_action_sets() are not accepted as selectable actions. Use their individual members instead.

For example, after permitting three total actions per unit, a second rule can allow at most one from the restoration/control subset:

subset_capacity <- problem |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(3, "max") |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(1, "max", actions = c("restore", "control"))

The remaining capacity can be used for fencing and monitoring. A rule that only counts an action subset does not replace the default total maximum; the explicit total bound in the first call is therefore necessary here.

Exact counts and combined bounds 

exact <- problem |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(2, "equal", pu = 10L) |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(0, "equal", pu = 20L)

Unit 10 must select exactly two actions; unit 20 cannot select any. An exact total count, like a total maximum, replaces the default one-action limit in its scoped units. A minimum alone retains that default. To require at least two actions while allowing up to four, supply both bounds:

bounded <- problem |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(4, "max", pu = 10L) |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(2, "min", pu = 10L)

All explicit rules apply together, independently of call order. If a maximum of four covers units 10 and 20, and a maximum of two covers units 20 and 30, the effective capacities are four, two, and two:

overlapping <- problem |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(4, "max", pu = c(10L, 20L)) |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(2, "max", pu = c(20L, 30L))

A later call does not overwrite an earlier rule. Reusing exactly the same planning-unit subset, action subset, and sense is rejected. Constraint names must also be unique within these rules. name labels a constraint for inspection; objective aliases continue to identify objectives in MO methods.

Available actions and infeasibility

Only available planning-unit/action pairs are counted. An action that is locked out or has an invalid cost is excluded as in model compilation. Locked-in actions remain individual selected decisions and count toward the bound. A positive minimum or equality larger than the available count in any scoped unit is rejected. Empty sums are zero: upper bounds and zero bounds remain valid for units without available actions.

Several individually valid rules can still conflict, or conflict with budgets and locked decisions. The solver reports that infeasibility. For example, a minimum of two combined with a maximum of one has no feasible allocation; adding a minimum does not silently change the upper bound.

Solve a cost/profit example

This example uses independent economic returns. Four actions in unit 10, two in unit 20, and one in unit 30 are optimal when every action has positive profit and no other resource limit applies:

economic <- capacities |>
  add_profit(c(restore = 8, control = 4, fence = 2, monitor = 1)) |>
  add_objective_max_profit(alias = "profit")
if (requireNamespace("rcbc", quietly = TRUE)) {
  solution <- solve(set_solver_cbc(economic, verbose = FALSE, gap_limit = 0))
  selected <- get_actions(solution)
  selected <- selected[selected$selected > 0.5, , drop = FALSE]
  stats::aggregate(selected ~ pu, selected, sum)
  get_objectives(solution)
}
#>   solution_id profit
#> 1           1     35

The maximum profit is 35: 15 from unit 10, 12 from unit 20, and 8 from unit 30. Action costs remain associated with each selected action, while planning-unit costs are charged once for each selected unit. Budgets and net-profit objectives use those same existing cost definitions. The three MO methods retain the cardinality constraints while exploring their objectives.

Capacity alone does not specify dependencies or compatibility. Add logical relations to require companion actions, exclude incompatible actions, or select an entire group together; see the action-relations vignette. These relations preserve the capacities configured here.

Ecological effects with concurrent actions

Concurrent individual effects are additive unless supplied joint effects specify a different total; see the joint-effects vignette. Benefit maximizes signed change, including negative effects. Loss measures deterioration after combining all scoped actions within each unit and feature. Solution summaries and ecological targets count the selected reference once.

ecological <- create_problem(
  data.frame(id = 10L, cost = 0), data.frame(id = 1L, name = "habitat"),
  data.frame(pu = 10L, feature = 1L, amount = 100)
) |>
  add_actions(data.frame(id = c("restore", "control")), cost = 1) |>
  add_constraint_action_cardinality(2, "equal") |>
  add_effects(data.frame(action = c("restore", "control"),
                        feature = "habitat", effect = c(30, -20))) |>
  add_constraint_targets_absolute(110) |>
  add_objective_max_effect(alias = "benefit")
solution <- solve(set_solver_cbc(ecological, gap_limit = 0, verbose = FALSE))
get_objectives(solution)
#>   solution_id benefit
#> 1           1      10
get_features(solution)
#>   feature feature_name baseline_total selected_baseline selected_amount_after
#> 1       1      habitat            100               100                   110
#>   selected_benefit selected_loss selected_net selected_fraction_of_baseline
#> 1               10             0           10                           1.1
stopifnot(get_objectives(solution)$benefit == 10,
          get_features(solution)$selected_loss == 0,
          get_features(solution)$selected_baseline == 100,
          get_features(solution)$selected_amount_after == 110)

The net change is +10, the final loss is zero, and the outcome is 110. The negative individual contribution is included before the final loss is split. Existing workflows with at most one action per unit retain that capacity; max_benefit() now includes negative effects in those workflows as well.
